summary: DHCP clients may try to update the same DNS name or one added for another purpose, causing conflicts. To resolve them, RFC 4703 proposes storing client identifiers in the DNS. This memo defines the DHCID resource record type for that purpose. It was later updated by RFC 5494.

plainLanguage.summary: When a computer gets its address over DHCP, the DNS entry for its name can be updated automatically. Two computers can then want the same name, and nothing in the DNS says which one owns it. This document defines a DNS record that holds a fingerprint of the DHCP client beside the name. The fingerprint is a one-way hash, so it does not expose the client's identity.

questions: dns record for dhcp client identifier
how is the dhcid hash computed
how do dhcp and dns avoid name conflicts
subtitle: A DNS record that stores a hashed DHCP client identity next to a name, so updaters can tell whose name it is.

tldr.problem: When DHCP clients or servers update DNS automatically, several clients may want the same name, or a name may already exist for another purpose, and nothing in the DNS says who owns it.
tldr.mechanism: The DHCID record, type code 49, holds a 2-octet identifier type, a 1-octet digest type and a SHA-256 hash of the client's identifier together with the domain name.
tldr.outcome: Updaters compare the stored hash with one they compute and, if it differs, treat the name as belonging to another client and follow site policy. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 5494.

facts.label: Unknown bits in the hash input

today: RFC 4701 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2006. It has not been obsoleted, but it was updated by RFC 5494.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4703 proposes a set of procedures that allow DHCP clients and servers to update the DNS automatically. Conflicts can arise if multiple DHCP clients wish to use the same DNS name, or if a DHCP client attempts to use a name that was added to the DNS for another purpose. To resolve such conflicts, RFC 4703 proposes storing client identifiers in the DNS, so that domain names can be associated unambiguously with the DHCP clients using them.

Because the DHCP information is easier to interpret when it has a resource record type of its own, this memo defines that record: the DHCID RR. DNS software should consider the RDATA section to be opaque. DHCP clients or servers use the DHCID RR to associate a DHCP client's identity with a DNS name, so that multiple DHCP clients and servers may deterministically perform dynamic DNS updates to the same zone.

To obscure potentially sensitive client identifying information, the data stored is the result of a one-way SHA-256 hash computation. The hash includes information from the DHCP client's message as well as the domain name itself, so the data stored in the DHCID RR depends on both the client identification used in the DHCP protocol interaction and the domain name. The DHCID RDATA therefore varies if a single client is associated over time with more than one name, which makes it difficult to track a client as it moves between various domain names.
sections.plainLanguage: When a computer gets its address over DHCP, the DNS entry for its name can be updated automatically. Two computers can then want the same name, and nothing in the DNS says which one owns it. This document defines a DNS record that holds a fingerprint of the DHCP client beside the name. The fingerprint is a one-way hash, so it does not expose the client's identity.

sections.title: The DHCID RDATA Format
sections.content:
The DHCID RR is defined with the mnemonic DHCID and type code 49. It is only defined in the IN class, and DHCID RRs cause no additional section processing.

The RDATA section of a DHCID RR in transmission contains RDLENGTH octets of binary data. From the updater's perspective, the RDATA consists of a 2-octet identifier type, in network byte order, followed by a 1-octet digest type, followed by one or more octets representing the actual identifier.

In DNS master files, the RDATA is represented as a single block in base-64 encoding, identical to that used for representing binary data in RFC 3548. The data may be divided into any number of white-space-separated substrings, down to single base-64 digits, which are concatenated to form the complete RDATA, and these substrings can span lines using the standard parentheses.
sections.plainLanguage: The record has three parts: a 2-octet field saying where the client identifier came from, a 1-octet field naming the hash algorithm, and the hash itself. In a zone file the whole thing is written as one base-64 block, which may be split across lines.

sections.title: Identifier and Digest Type Codes
sections.content:
The identifier type code says what data from the DHCP client's request was used as input into the hash function. The codes live in a registry maintained by IANA, and the initial list assigns three values.

  • 0x0000: the 1-octet htype followed by hlen octets of chaddr from a DHCPv4 client's DHCPREQUEST.
  • 0x0001: the data octets, that is the Type and Client-Identifier fields, from a DHCPv4 client's Client Identifier option.
  • 0x0002: the client's DUID, that is the data octets of a DHCPv6 client's Client Identifier option, or the DUID field from a DHCPv4 client's Client Identifier option.
  • 0x0003 to 0xfffe are undefined and available to be assigned by IANA, and 0xffff is undefined and reserved.

The digest type code is an identifier for the digest algorithm used, and the digest is calculated over an identifier and the canonical FQDN. The digest type codes live in another IANA registry. Value 0 is reserved and value 1 is SHA-256. Reserving other types requires IETF standards action, and defining new values will also require IETF standards action to document how DNS updaters are to deal with multiple digest types.
sections.plainLanguage: The first field says which part of the DHCP message identifies the client: the hardware address, the DHCPv4 client identifier option, or the DUID. The second field names the hash algorithm, and today only SHA-256 is assigned. Both fields are registries that IANA maintains.

sections.title: Computation of the RDATA
sections.content:
The DHCID RDATA is formed by concatenating the 2-octet identifier type code with variable-length data. For all type codes other than 0xffff, which is reserved for future expansion, the RDATA is the 2-octet identifier type code, the 1-octet digest type code, and the digest value, which is 32 octets for SHA-256.

The input to the digest hash function is the identifier followed by the FQDN. The FQDN is represented in the buffer in the canonical wire format described in RFC 4034, Section 6.2, and the identifier type code describes the source of the identifier.

A DHCPv4 updater uses the 0x0002 type code if a Client Identifier option is present in the DHCPv4 messages and it is encoded as specified in RFC 4361. Otherwise, the updater uses 0x0001 if a Client Identifier option is present, and 0x0000 if not. A DHCPv6 updater always uses the 0x0002 type code.

When the identifier is the DUID, the first two octets of the DHCID RR MUST be 0x0002 in network byte order, the third octet is the digest type code, and the rest MUST contain the results of computing the SHA-256 hash across the octets of the DUID followed by the FQDN. When the identifier is the DHCPv4 Client Identifier option sent by the client in its DHCPREQUEST message, the first two octets MUST be 0x0001, the third octet is the digest type code, and the rest MUST contain the results of hashing the data octets of the option followed by the FQDN. When the identifier is the client's link-layer address, the first two octets MUST be zero, the third octet is the digest type code, and the updater computes the hash over a buffer containing the client's network hardware type as it appeared in the DHCP htype field, all of the significant octets of the chaddr field in the same order as in the DHCPREQUEST message, whose number is given by the hlen field, and then the FQDN data.
sections.plainLanguage: The hash is computed over the client identifier followed by the name, with the name in its canonical DNS wire form. Which identifier is used depends on the protocol: a DHCPv6 updater always uses the DUID, while a DHCPv4 updater prefers the DUID form of the client identifier option, then the raw option, and finally the hardware address.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
Three examples show the record in use. In the first, a DHCP server allocates the IPv6 address 2001:DB8::1234:5678 to a client that included the DHCPv6 client-identifier option data 00:01:00:06:41:2d:f1:66:01:02:03:04:05:06 in its DHCPv6 request. The server updates the name chi6.example.com on the client's behalf and uses the client identifier option data as input, setting the two type octets to 0x0002, the digest type octet to 1 for SHA-256, and hashing the 14 octets from the option together with the FQDN.

In the second example, a server allocates 192.0.2.2 to a client that included the DHCP client-identifier option data 01:07:08:09:0a:0b:0c in its DHCP request. The name chi.example.com is updated, the two type octets are 0x0001, the digest type octet is 1, and the hash covers the seven octets from the option and the FQDN. In the third example, a server allocates 192.0.2.3 to a client with the Ethernet MAC address 01:02:03:04:05:06 using the domain name client.example.com. The two type octets are zero, the digest type octet is 1, and the hash covers the 1-octet htype value for Ethernet, 0x01, the six octets of the MAC address, and the domain name.

For servers that do not know the DHCID type, the same RDATA is written in the generic form defined in RFC 3597, which shows the length of 35 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: The three examples cover the three identifier types: a DHCPv6 client identifier, a DHCPv4 client identifier option, and a plain hardware address. Each produces a 35-octet record that is shown both as base-64 and in the generic form used by servers that do not know the type.

sections.title: Updater Behavior
sections.content:
The data in the DHCID RR allows updaters to determine whether more than one DHCP client desires to use a particular FQDN. This lets site administrators establish policy about DNS updates, but the DHCID RR does not establish any policy itself.

Updaters use data from a DHCP client's request and the domain name that the client wants to use to compute a client identity hash, and then compare that hash with the data in any DHCID RRs on the name that they wish to associate with the client's IP address. If an updater discovers DHCID RRs whose RDATA does not match the client identity that it has computed, the updater SHOULD conclude that a different client is currently associated with the name in question. The updater SHOULD then proceed according to the site's administrative policy, which might dictate that a different name be selected, or might permit the updater to continue.

This RR MUST NOT be used for any purpose other than the one detailed in RFC 4703. Although the record contains data that is opaque to DNS servers, the data must be consistent across all entities that update and interpret it, so new data formats may only be defined through actions of the DHC Working Group, as a result of revising RFC 4703.
sections.plainLanguage: The record does not decide anything by itself. It lets the updater work out whether the name is already held by a different client, and then the site's own policy decides whether to rename the new client or let it take the name.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The DHCID record as such does not introduce any new security problems into the DNS. A one-way hash is used to obscure the client's identity information, and the FQDN is included in the hash computation so that it is difficult to track a client by examining the names associated with a particular hash value. The RDATA is therefore dependent on both the DHCP client identification data and on each FQDN associated with the client.

An attacker that has some knowledge, such as of MAC addresses commonly used in DHCP client identification data, may be able to discover the client's DHCP identity by using a brute-force attack. Even without any additional knowledge, the number of unknown bits used in computing the hash is typically only 48 to 80.

Administrators should be wary of permitting unsecured DNS updates to zones, whether or not they are exposed to the global Internet. Both DHCP clients and servers SHOULD use some form of update authentication, such as the mechanism in RFC 2845, when performing DNS updates.
sections.plainLanguage: The hash hides the client's identity from anyone reading the DNS, but it is not a secret: an attacker who can guess a hardware address can confirm it by recomputing the hash. DNS updates to these zones should also be authenticated, so that only the rightful updater can change a name.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has allocated a DNS RR type number for the DHCID record type. This specification defines a new number space for the 2-octet identifier type codes associated with the DHCID RR, with three initial values assigned and the value 0xFFFF reserved for future use. It defines a second new number space for the 1-octet digest type codes, with two initial values assigned. New values in either space are assigned through Standards Action.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks IANA to register the record type and the two code spaces it uses: one for the client identifier source and one for the hash algorithm. New codes in either space need a Standards Action.

fields.name: Identifier type
fields.desc: Two octets in network byte order, naming where the client identifier came from.

fields.name: Digest type
fields.desc: One octet naming the hash algorithm. Value 1 is SHA-256.

fields.name: Digest
fields.desc: The hash value, 32 octets for SHA-256.

items.label: htype and chaddr
items.desc: The 1-octet htype followed by hlen octets of chaddr from a DHCPv4 client's DHCPREQUEST.

items.label: DHCPv4 Client Identifier option
items.desc: The data octets, that is the Type and Client-Identifier fields, from a DHCPv4 client's Client Identifier option.

items.label: Client DUID
items.desc: The client's DUID, from a DHCPv6 Client Identifier option or the DUID field of a DHCPv4 Client Identifier option.

viz.caption: WHAT AN UPDATER DOES WITH A DHCID RECORD

items.title: Compute
items.text: Hash the client's identifier together with the name it wants.

items.title: Compare
items.text: Check the hash against the DHCID records already on that name.

items.title: Decide
items.text: A different hash means another client already holds the name.

items.title: Apply policy
items.text: The record sets no policy; the site does.
